items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: He was musical director for his wife Pearl Bailey, until the time of her death

ctx.x: Drummer and arranger Louie Bellson is one of the most recorded musicians in jazz. He learned piano, percussion and music theory as a youth and won a drum contest sponsored by Gene Krupa at the age of 16. One year later he was playing with Benny Goodman and soon after developed the double bass drum set that has become his trademark. Louis has propelled the big bands of Tommy Dorsey, Count Basie, and Harry James, and enjoyed a long and fruitful association with Duke Ellington, who performed some of the drummer’s…
Louie was interviewed by Monk Rowe on April 12, 1996 at the Sarasota Jazz Festival.

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Meeting Pearl. Because I couldn’t do both. When she was busy doing her things, and I became the musical conductor for her – and I had Don Redman as the bandleader.

ctx.x: And you left. What were the circumstances of your departure?

Meeting Pearl. Because I couldn’t do both. When she was busy doing her things, and I became the musical conductor for her – and I had Don Redman as the bandleader. There’s a name. There was another genius. Him and Benny Carter wrote most of the tunes for Pearl. Don Redman. Again, there was a tiny man, but a genius. Chant of the Weed.
Yeah, it goes all the way back to McKinney’s Cotton Pickers.
